title: The 10 R-Strategies of the Circular Economy
definition: The ten strategies are classified under three categories that demonstrate the length of the waste loop each represents. The shorter the loop, the more sustainable the strategy is.

categories.name: Short Loops: Smarter Product Use and Manufacturing
categories.note: Most sustainable — least material and energy re-processing.

strategies.name: Refuse
strategies.description: Either bans the use of specific materials deemed harmful to the planet, puts an end to a certain production process, or phases out one product that is detrimental to the environment in favour of an efficient alternative.

strategies.name: Rethink
strategies.description: Making a product use-intensive through sharing products or by putting multi-functional products on the market (e.g. leasing clothes, battery swapping points, or reusable coffee mugs).

strategies.name: Reduce
strategies.description: Aims to increase the efficiency of product manufacturing or use. Doing so results in using fewer natural resources and producing less waste.

categories.name: Medium Loops: Extend the Lifespan of a Product and Its Parts

strategies.name: Reuse
strategies.description: When a different consumer uses a discarded product that is still in good condition and is able to fulfil its original function.

strategies.name: Repair
strategies.description: The Repair and maintenance of a defective product so it can perform once more.

strategies.name: Refurbish
strategies.description: Restoring an old product and bringing it up to date. Upgrading or modernising a product can happen within (with updated components) and on the outside.

strategies.name: Remanufacture
strategies.description: Involves integrating product components that are still perfectly intact into new products with the same function.

strategies.name: Repurpose
strategies.description: Incorporates discarded components into a completely different product for a unique benefit or alternative purpose.

categories.name: Long Loops: Creative Material Application
categories.note: Least sustainable of the R-strategies — material is broken down before reuse.

strategies.name: Recycle
strategies.description: Processing materials through recycling makes sense, especially when a product cannot be used any longer and there are materials within it to recover.

strategies.name: Recover
strategies.description: The composting of organic waste can recover energy through anaerobic digestion or waste-to-energy incineration that generates electricity or heat.

enablers.name: Design for circularity
enablers.description: Durability, modularity, recyclability, and disassembly designed into the product so downstream R-strategies become possible.

enablers.name: R&D and innovation
enablers.description: Research into circular materials, processes, and technologies (e.g. recycled feedstock, bio-based inputs).

enablers.name: Digital and data infrastructure
enablers.description: Digital product passports, material traceability, IoT tracking, and the data systems that make loops auditable.

enablers.name: Workforce skills and training
enablers.description: Building the skills and capability needed to repair, refurbish, and run circular operations.

enablers.name: Partnerships and collaboration
enablers.description: Value-chain collaboration, take-back networks, industry consortia, and customer engagement.

enablers.name: Reverse logistics
enablers.description: Collection, take-back, and sorting infrastructure that returns used products and materials into loops.

enablers.name: Circular finance and business models
enablers.description: Financing circular business models (product-as-a-service, leasing) and capital for circular production lines.

enablers.name: Policy and standards engagement
enablers.description: Policy advocacy and regulatory alignment such as extended producer responsibility and right-to-repair.
